title: IV Push Medications: Verify Before the Syringe
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: IV push medications can produce immediate toxicity because the full dose enters the circulation rapidly. Verify that the drug may be given IV push, the concentration and rate, line patency/compatibility, patient-specific contraindications, and required monitoring before administration.
recognize: A drug ordered IV does not automatically mean IV push is an approved route.
Rate errors can cause hypotension, dysrhythmia, respiratory depression, or tissue injury before there is time to correct the mistake.
priorities: Verify medication, concentration, route, rate, dilution requirements, line compatibility, and patient monitoring.
Confirm a patent vascular access device appropriate for the medication.
Stop and escalate immediately for acute reaction, severe pain/swelling, or cardiopulmonary deterioration.
assessMonitor: Monitor medication-specific vital signs, rhythm, respiratory status, sedation, infusion site, and clinical response.
interventions: Use the approved administration reference and facility policy rather than memory for IV-push rate/dilution.
Label prepared syringes immediately when not administered at once.
medicationSafety: Never IV-push potassium-containing replacement solutions.
IV push authority for LPN/LVN practice varies by state, medication, and facility competency.
teaching: Explain immediate symptoms that should be reported during or after administration, such as burning, dizziness, chest symptoms, or breathing difficulty.
delegationScope: IV push administration is state/facility/medication specific for LPN/LVN practice; never assume universal authority.
examTrap: Giving a medication rapidly because the order says IV without checking whether IV push is permitted and at what rate.
oneLinePearl: IV route is not the same thing as IV push permission.
sourceBasis: FDA product labeling and facility IV-push policy

title: IV Piggyback: Compatibility and Line Control
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Secondary IV medications are only safe when the drug, diluent, concentration, line, primary fluid, Y-site compatibility, pump settings, and flush plan are correct. Do not assume two medications are compatible because both are commonly given intravenously.
recognize: Precipitation, cloudiness, color change, unexpected line occlusion, or patient reaction can signal incompatibility or preparation error.
A secondary bag connected incorrectly can fail to infuse while the primary fluid continues.
priorities: Verify compatibility from an approved source before connecting to an existing line.
Program the pump and secondary setup correctly and confirm the intended bag is actually infusing.
Flush according to medication/line protocol when sequential incompatible medications share access.
assessMonitor: Inspect tubing/solution, infusion site, pump display, remaining volume, and medication-specific patient response.
interventions: Use dedicated access when required for incompatible or high-risk medications.
Trace tubing from patient to solution before starting or changing infusions.
medicationSafety: Compatibility is specific to drug, concentration, diluent, and contact conditions.
Never rely on memory alone for uncertain Y-site compatibility.
redFlags: High-risk drug connected to the wrong line
teaching: Tell patients to report burning, swelling, wetness, or pain at the IV site promptly.
delegationScope: IV medication administration authority varies by state/facility for LPN/LVN practice; compatibility verification remains a medication-safety responsibility.
examTrap: Assuming the existing primary IV fluid is compatible with a new antibiotic because both are clear solutions.
oneLinePearl: Trace the line, prove compatibility, then program the pump.

title: High-Alert Infusions: Pump and Independent Check
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
bottomLine: High-alert infusions such as insulin, heparin, vasopressors, concentrated electrolytes, and certain sedatives require reliable pump programming, standardized concentrations when available, line tracing, and independent double checks when policy requires them.
recognize: Dose-unit mismatches, wrong concentration selection, decimal errors, and wrong-channel programming can create large dosing errors even when the medication name is correct.
Smart-pump alerts are safety signals, not obstacles to bypass automatically.
priorities: Match order, concentration, patient weight when relevant, dosing units, channel, line, and pump library entry.
Complete required independent verification without coaching the checker toward the first calculation.
Investigate unexpected pump alerts or unusually high/low calculated rates.
assessMonitor: Trend medication-specific endpoints such as glucose, aPTT/anti-Xa when ordered, BP, rhythm, sedation, urine output, and infusion-site status.
interventions: Label lines and pumps clearly and trace from bag to patient during handoff.
Use standardized concentrations and dose-error-reduction software when available.
medicationSafety: A pump does not make an incorrect dose safe.
Never bypass a dose-limit alert without resolving why the programmed dose exceeds the expected range.
redFlags: Clinical deterioration after a rate change
teaching: Explain that frequent monitoring is expected with high-alert infusions because doses may be adjusted to response.
delegationScope: High-alert infusion management is competency- and policy-specific and may exceed LPN/LVN scope in some jurisdictions/settings.
examTrap: Trusting the smart pump as proof that the entered dose and concentration are correct.
oneLinePearl: Smart pump plus wrong input is still a wrong dose.
sourceBasis: ISMP high-alert medication and smart-pump safety principles

title: PCA Opioids: Only the Patient Pushes
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Patient-controlled analgesia is designed so the capable patient activates doses. Family members or staff must not perform PCA-by-proxy unless a separate clinician-controlled protocol specifically authorizes it; sedation and respiratory status are more important than pain score alone.
recognize: Increasing sedation often precedes serious opioid-induced respiratory depression.
Sleep apnea, older age, opioid-naive status, concurrent sedatives, renal/hepatic impairment, or supplemental oxygen can alter risk recognition.
priorities: Assess sedation, respiratory rate/quality, oxygenation, pain, and ability to understand PCA use.
Verify pump settings, concentration, lockout, and basal infusion only when specifically ordered.
Stop/escalate per protocol for excessive sedation or respiratory depression and prepare naloxone when indicated.
assessMonitor: Trend sedation using a standardized scale, respirations, oxygenation, pain, total dose attempts/deliveries, and adverse effects.
interventions: Teach that only the patient presses the button.
Use continuous monitoring when required by patient risk and facility policy.
medicationSafety: Supplemental oxygen can mask hypoventilation if only SpO2 is watched; assess ventilation and sedation.
Concurrent benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants increase risk.
teaching: Only the patient should activate the PCA button; family should call staff if pain is uncontrolled or the patient becomes too sleepy.
delegationScope: PCA assessment and pump management require licensed clinical competency; scope varies by state/facility.
examTrap: Allowing a family member to push the PCA button while the patient sleeps.
oneLinePearl: With PCA, sedation is the warning sign and only the patient pushes.

title: Enteral Tube Medications: Do Not Crush Everything
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Medication administration through a feeding tube requires verification that each formulation can be crushed/opened and delivered through that tube. Extended-release, delayed-release, enteric-coated, hazardous, or special-formulation products may be unsafe to crush.
recognize: Tube occlusion, altered drug absorption, dose dumping, or occupational exposure can result from inappropriate crushing.
Medication-feed interactions can reduce absorption for selected drugs.
priorities: Verify tube type/location and that the medication formulation is suitable for enteral-tube administration.
Give medications separately rather than mixing an entire medication pass into formula.
Flush before, between, and after medications according to patient/fluid restrictions and policy.
assessMonitor: Monitor tube patency, medication effect, GI tolerance, hydration/fluid restrictions, and interaction-specific labs or drug levels.
interventions: Request a liquid or alternate formulation when tablets/capsules cannot be safely modified.
Pause feedings only when the medication-specific evidence/order requires it.
medicationSafety: Do not crush extended-release, enteric-coated, sublingual/buccal, or hazardous products unless an approved source specifically permits manipulation.
Check liquid osmolality/sorbitol burden when diarrhea occurs.
redFlags: Acute toxicity after crushed modified-release medication
teaching: Caregivers should verify every medication before crushing it for a feeding tube; appearance alone does not prove crushability.
delegationScope: Medication-formulation verification and administration remain licensed responsibilities within scope; feeding assistance does not transfer medication judgment.
examTrap: Crushing all tablets together because the patient cannot swallow them.
oneLinePearl: Tube access changes the route, not the medication's formulation rules.

title: Insulin Mixing and Meal Timing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Insulin errors often come from confusing type, concentration, timing, or meal relationship. Verify the exact insulin product and glucose context; do not mix insulin glargine, detemir, or degludec with other insulins, and coordinate rapid/short-acting insulin with reliable carbohydrate intake according to the order.
recognize: Look-alike insulin names and multiple concentrations increase selection risk.
Unexpected NPO status, vomiting, delayed trays, or reduced intake can turn an otherwise correct mealtime dose into hypoglycemia.
priorities: Check glucose and confirm the exact insulin, concentration, dose, route, and timing.
Confirm meal availability/ability to eat for nutritional insulin.
Use required independent double checks and standardized devices.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, intake, hypoglycemia symptoms, potassium in high-dose IV insulin situations, and response to regimen.
interventions: If mixing compatible regular and NPH insulin when specifically ordered, follow facility technique and product guidance.
Keep insulin pens patient-specific and never share pens between patients.
medicationSafety: Long-acting analogs such as glargine, detemir, and degludec are not mixed in the same syringe with other insulins.
Do not administer nutritional insulin and then discover the patient cannot eat without immediately addressing the mismatch.
teaching: Know insulin names, devices, meal timing, and hypoglycemia treatment; never share insulin pens.
delegationScope: Insulin administration/adjustment authority varies by setting and state; assessment of abnormal glucose trends is a licensed responsibility.
examTrap: Giving rapid-acting insulin before confirming that the patient can receive and eat the meal.
oneLinePearl: Insulin safety is product + concentration + glucose + meal timing.
sourceBasis: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Subcutaneous Anticoagulants: Inject, Do Not Massage
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Subcutaneous heparin and LMWH are administered with bleeding-focused safety. Use the product-specific technique, rotate sites, avoid massaging the injection area, and monitor platelet count/renal function when clinically indicated.
recognize: Bruising at injection sites can occur, but expanding hematoma, hematuria, melena, severe headache, or hemodynamic change can signal significant bleeding.
LMWH accumulation risk increases with renal impairment.
priorities: Verify drug, dose, indication, renal function context, platelet trend, and bleeding risk.
Use the abdomen/site and syringe technique specified by the product/facility.
Do not massage after injection.
assessMonitor: Trend bleeding, platelet count, hemoglobin when ordered, renal function, and injection-site hematoma.
interventions: Rotate sites and avoid injecting into bruised, scarred, inflamed, or compromised tissue.
medicationSafety: Do not expel a manufacturer-provided prefilled syringe air bubble unless product instructions say to do so.
HIT can occur with heparin products and requires immediate escalation.
teaching: Report black stools, red urine, unusual bleeding, severe headache, or large unexplained bruises.
delegationScope: Anticoagulant administration follows scope; evaluation of bleeding/HIT concerns requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Massaging the injection site after LMWH administration to reduce discomfort.
oneLinePearl: Subcutaneous anticoagulant: rotate, inject, don't massage, watch bleeding and platelets.

title: Transdermal Patches: Remove the Old Dose First
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Transdermal systems continue delivering medication for hours or days, so an old patch left in place can create an unintended overdose. Remove the previous system, verify site/date/time, avoid heat unless specifically permitted, and fold/dispose used patches safely because active drug may remain.
recognize: Patch-related overdose may present as medication-specific toxicity, such as opioid sedation or nitrate hypotension.
Heating pads, fever, or external heat can increase absorption for some transdermal systems.
priorities: Locate and remove the prior patch before applying the new one.
Inspect skin and rotate sites according to product instructions.
Document site and application/removal time.
assessMonitor: Monitor skin reaction and medication-specific effects such as BP, pain, sedation, or smoking-withdrawal symptoms.
interventions: Fold used patches adhesive-to-adhesive and dispose according to product/facility instructions.
medicationSafety: Do not cut a transdermal system unless the specific product is designed and labeled for cutting.
Avoid external heat unless product instructions explicitly permit it.
teaching: Check that the old patch is off before applying the new one and keep used patches away from children and pets.
delegationScope: Medication administration is a licensed task within scope; routine skin observation may support but not replace medication assessment.
examTrap: Applying a new patch without first locating the old one.
oneLinePearl: Patch safety starts with finding and removing yesterday's dose.
sourceBasis: FDA transdermal-system labeling and medication-safety principles

title: Eye-Drop Administration: Protect the Cornea and Dose
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Correct eye-drop technique protects the cornea, prevents contamination, and improves dosing. Instill into the conjunctival sac without touching the tip to the eye, close the eye gently, and use nasolacrimal occlusion when appropriate to reduce systemic absorption.
recognize: Touching the dropper tip to lashes or eye contaminates the bottle and can injure the cornea.
Multiple drops placed rapidly can wash the first medication out rather than increasing effect.
priorities: Verify the correct eye and medication.
Retract the lower lid and instill into the conjunctival sac rather than directly on the cornea.
Separate different ophthalmic medications by the prescribed interval.
assessMonitor: Monitor eye redness, pain, drainage, visual change, and ability to self-administer.
interventions: Use gloves when drainage/infection precautions require them and avoid cross-contaminating bilateral eye care.
medicationSafety: Punctal occlusion can reduce systemic absorption of drugs such as topical beta blockers.
Do not let the dropper tip contact the eye, fingers, or other surfaces.
teaching: Wash hands, avoid touching the tip, use the correct eye, and wait the instructed time between different drops.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows scope; acute eye findings require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Dropping medication directly onto the cornea or touching the bottle tip to the eyelashes.
oneLinePearl: Conjunctival sac, clean tip, gentle closure, punctal pressure when appropriate.

title: Ear Drops: Age, Temperature, and Technique
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Otic medication technique depends on age and tympanic-membrane status. Warm drops in the hands, position the affected ear upward, straighten the canal appropriately for age, avoid contaminating the tip, and verify that the product is safe when perforation or ear tubes are present.
recognize: Cold ear drops can provoke vertigo or nausea.
Severe pain, mastoid swelling, neurologic symptoms, or sudden hearing loss is not routine otitis externa care.
priorities: Verify the correct ear and medication.
For adults/older children, pull the pinna up and back; for young children, use the age-appropriate down-and-back technique per facility teaching.
Keep the treated ear upward for the instructed time.
assessMonitor: Monitor pain, drainage, hearing change, dizziness, fever, and ability to self-administer.
interventions: Warm the container in the hands rather than using unsafe external heating.
Do not insert the dropper deeply into the canal.
medicationSafety: Some otic preparations are not appropriate with a perforated tympanic membrane or tympanostomy tube; verify the product/order.
Do not use ophthalmic/otic products interchangeably unless specifically prescribed and confirmed.
teaching: Warm drops in your hand, use the correct ear technique, and report severe dizziness, hearing loss, or worsening pain.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows scope; severe ear or neurologic findings require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Using the adult up-and-back technique for every child regardless of age.
oneLinePearl: Warm drops and straighten the canal for the patient's age.
